method: COMPILED FROM 3 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome' (2025), 18 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at PMC JATS XML <license> element for PMC12483350 (NCBI efetch; Europe PMC returned 503)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535) 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care' (November 2025), 7 claims; LICENCE: © The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners 2025 (free to read; no open licence stated) (read at the article PDF from racgp.org.au (copyright line on every page; Unpaywall lists it as free to read without a licence)). S3: QUOTED from Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352) 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide' (published 16 November 2025), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12686656). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds management. S2 (AJGP 2025) is the Australian primary-care approach to hypertriglyceridaemia: © RACGP, free to read, so paraphrased and hash-anchored. S3 (Bajaj et al. 2025) is an FCS treatment review, CC BY, quoted; it was funded by Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the maker of olezarsen, and two authors are Ionis employees. No FCS management guideline was readable: the NLA 2025 expert review and the 2018 dietary recommendations (J Clin Lipidol) returned a bot challenge in Wave 5. The S1 claims are unchanged. Source text for S1: NCBI efetch JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 503 on 2026-09-23). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 1 (the Mouline FCS score). S1 Table 2 and S3 Table 2 have merged cells and S3 Table 1 a multi-row header, so they were not extracted.

claims.claim: **FCS is a rare recessive disorder** (about 1 to 10 per million) caused by biallelic variants affecting lipoprotein lipase (LPL). It carries a high risk of recurrent, life-threatening acute pancreatitis.
claims.source_text: FCS is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects approximately 1 to 10 individuals per million and is caused by biallelic pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants in the genes encoding the lipoprotein lipase (LPL) enzyme. In addition to its heterogeneous clinical presentation, FCS is characterized by a greater risk of life-threatening, recurrent acute pancreatitis and type 3 diabetes
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis starts with finding severe hypertriglyceridaemia.** Some patients have few or no symptoms. Triglycerides are extremely and persistently high (above 885 mg/dL).
claims.source_text: While some patients present with mild or no symptoms, the diagnostic process begins with the detection of severe hypertriglyceridemia (HTG). … The diagnosis of FCS is largely based on the identification of extreme and persistent elevations in plasma or serum levels of TGs (>885 mg/dL)
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A poor response to standard lipid-lowering drugs is typical,** and FCS is widely underdiagnosed, which delays proper treatment.
claims.source_text: A poor response to conventional lipid-lowering therapies is common among these patients because of impaired lipid clearance. However, FCS remains largely underdiagnosed, which may lead to delayed initiation of adequate treatment
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Most chylomicronaemia is not FCS:** polygenic and secondary causes are 40 to 60 times more likely than monogenic ones such as FCS or familial partial lipodystrophy.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Suspect a monogenic cause when triglycerides are extremely high (for example above 10 mmol/L) with features in childhood or adolescence,** or when a sibling has severe hypertriglyceridaemia. Refer to a specialist, especially when no secondary cause is found.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Severe hypertriglyceridaemia is 5.6 mmol/L or more,** fasting or not. At that level the priority moves from cardiovascular risk to preventing acute pancreatitis, which can be fatal.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Look for and correct secondary causes:** poorly controlled diabetes, insulin resistance, central obesity, diets high in simple carbohydrate or saturated fat, heavy drinking and some medicines.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Use a clinical score** to support the diagnosis and to separate FCS from multifactorial chylomicronaemia (MCS). (100% agreement)
claims.source_text: the expert panel recommends the use of clinical scores for the diagnosis of FCS. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). … Available pragmatic scores for the diagnosis of FCS, which rely mainly on clinical parameters (Tables 1 and 2), may assist in differentiating between FCS and multifactorial chylomicronemia syndrome (MCS)
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The FCS (Mouline) score, S1 Table 1:** fasting triglycerides above 885 mg/dL on at least three consecutive measurements taken at least one month apart (+5), and above 1,770 mg/dL at least once (+1); any earlier triglyceride below 177 mg/dL (−5); no secondary factor, apart from pregnancy and ethinylestradiol use (+2); past pancreatitis (+1); unexplained recurrent abdominal pain (+1); no familial combined hyperlipidaemia (+1); triglycerides falling by less than 20% on lipid-lowering treatment (+1); symptom onset before 40 years (+1), before 20 (+2) or before 10 (+3).
claims.source_text: [Table 1 row 1] Criteria: Fasting TG levels >885 mg/dL on at least three consecutive measurements ( * ) Fasting TG levels >1,770 mg/dL at least once · Score: +5 +1 [Table 1 row 2] Criteria: Previous TG levels <177 mg/dL at least once · Score: -5 [Table 1 row 3] Criteria: Absence of secondary factors (†) (except for pregnancy (‡) and use of ethinylestradiol) · Score: +2 [Table 1 row 4] Criteria: History of pancreatitis · Score: +1 [Table 1 row 5] Criteria: Unexplained recurrent abdominal pain · Score: +1 [Table 1 row 6] Criteria: No history of familial combined hyperlipidemia · Score: +1 [Table 1 row 7] Criteria: No response (TG levels decreased by <20%) to lipid-lowering treatment · Score: +1 [Table 1 row 8] Criteria: Age at symptom onset <40 years <20 years <10 years · Score: +1 +2 +3 … ( * ) Measurements performed at least one month apart.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Reading the Mouline score:** 10 or more makes FCS very likely, 9 or less unlikely and 8 or less very unlikely. Secondary factors are alcohol, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, corticosteroid treatment and other drugs. A diagnosis made in pregnancy needs a second test after delivery.
claims.source_text: [Table 1 row 9] Criteria: Score ≥10: FCS is very likely Score ≤9: FCS is unlikely · Score: Score ≤8: FCS is very unlikely … (†) Alcohol, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, corticotherapy, and the use of other drugs. (‡) If the diagnosis is made during pregnancy, a second test will be required to confirm the diagnosis postpartum.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Features that point to FCS:** no secondary cause of severe hypertriglyceridaemia; past pancreatitis; no response to standard treatment; recurrent unexplained abdominal pain; onset in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood.
claims.source_text: [3.1] Absence of secondary factors for severe HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.2] History of pancreatitis. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.3] Refractoriness to conventional treatments for HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.4] A history of unexplained recurrent abdominal pain due to other reasons. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.5] Early disease onset (childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood).
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Typical lipid profile:** normal or low LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, a triglyceride-to-total-cholesterol ratio above 5, and low-to-normal apoB. Diabetes appearing after the lipid diagnosis also fits (75% agreement).
claims.source_text: [3.6] Consistent lipid profile (normal or low levels of direct low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C], low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [HDL-C], TG/total cholesterol (TC) ratio >5, and low-to-normal levels of apolipoprotein B [apoB]). … [3.7] Onset of diabetes following the diagnosis of HTG. Expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 75%).
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Body weight does not rule it out:** a normal BMI may be a clue, but FCS occurs in normal-weight and overweight people.
claims.source_text: a normal body mass index (BMI) might serve as a useful indicator; however, both normal-weight and overweight individuals can develop FCS
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genes to test first:** LPL, GPIHBP1 and APOA5, then APOC2 and LMF1. LPL variants explain 50–90% of cases, depending on the population.
claims.source_text: [4.1] LPL. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [4.2] GPIHBP1. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [4.3] APOA5. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 83.3%). [4.4] APOC2. Expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 75%). [4.5] LMF1. … Depending on the target population, 50-90% of patients with FCS may have biallelic variants in the LPL gene
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genetic testing is the preferred way to confirm FCS.** Where it is not available, clinical assessment including scores is the best practical method.
claims.source_text: under ideal circumstances, genetic testing is the recommended method to confirm the diagnosis of FCS. … under real-world circumstances, the clinical evaluation of the patient (including clinical scores) is the best diagnostic method for FCS.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A negative genetic test does not exclude FCS:** nearly 25% of patients with a typical picture test negative.
claims.source_text: nearly 25% of patients presenting with clinical features consistent with FCS have a negative genetic test result
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If genetics are negative or show a variant of unknown significance, measure LPL activity** where available. Anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies or whole-exome sequencing are alternatives. Each laboratory sets its own cut-off; activity in FCS is usually 25% or less.
claims.source_text: the LPL activity assay (if available) should be conducted in patients with clinical features and laboratory findings consistent with FCS + a negative genetic test or a variant of unknown significance (VUS). … this preferential recommendation does not preclude the use of other strategies, such as the identification of anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies or whole-exome sequencing. … Each laboratory should set their own cutoff values to measure LPL activity, which is typically ≤25% of said value among patients with FCS
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A single heterozygous variant counts as a negative result,** as does a variant of unknown significance in these genes.
claims.source_text: the presence of heterozygous P/LP variants in a single canonical gene or the detection of homozygous or heterozygous VUS in the same genes are also regarded as negative genetic test results.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Definite FCS:** clinical, biochemical and genetic findings fit, and LPL activity is absent. **MCS:** findings fit but genetics are negative and LPL activity is normal.
claims.source_text: [14.1] Clinical, biochemical, and genetic testing consistent with FCS and absent LPL activity: diagnosis of FCS. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [14.2] Clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + negative genetic testing + normal LPL activity: diagnosis of MCS.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Possible FCS:** negative genetics with low LPL activity. **Probable FCS:** inconclusive genetics with low LPL activity. Inconclusive genetics with normal LPL activity suggests MCS.
claims.source_text: the possible diagnosis of FCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical features consistent with FCS + negative genetic tests + low LPL activity. … the probable diagnosis of FCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + inconclusive genetic tests + low LPL … the diagnosis of MCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + inconclusive genetic tests + normal LPL
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Think of autoimmune chylomicronaemia (anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies)** when hypertriglyceridaemia is intermittent, genetics are inconclusive, there are other autoimmune conditions, or onset is in adulthood.
claims.source_text: [12.1] Intermittent HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [12.2] Inconclusive genetic testing results. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [12.3] History of other autoimmune conditions. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 83.3%). [12.4] Adult onset. … Autoimmune chylomicronemia can be caused by the presence of anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use the same diagnostic approach** in patients admitted with acute pancreatitis, in pregnancy and in children (including those under 10).
claims.source_text: the diagnostic approach for FCS should not be changed under the following special circumstances: (a) patients hospitalized for acute pancreatitis; (b) pregnant patients; and (c) pediatric patients. … The diagnostic approach for patients aged under 10 years is comparable to that for adults
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The FCS diet is strict and lifelong:** under 15–20 g of fat a day, with simple carbohydrates and alcohol restricted, whatever drug is added. Monitor fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and supplement if needed.
claims.source_text: Regardless of adjunct pharmacologic treatment, patients with FCS must adhere to a strict, very low-fat FCS diet (<15-20 g fat/day) and restrict simple carbohydrates and alcohol, which can increase TG levels and trigger acute pancreatitis … Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) should be monitored and possibly supplemented in the FCS diet
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) do not drive chylomicron production and can be a good fat source,** but MCT oils can be expensive.
claims.source_text: Purified medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) do not promote chylomicron synthesis and may be a good source of fat [,]; while MCT oils are commercially available, they are potentially costly
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Ordinary 'low-fat' recipes and diabetes diets are often too fatty for FCS** (the aim is under 20 g/day). Work with a registered dietitian on a personalised plan.
claims.source_text: Standard "low-fat" recipes for patients with hypercholesterolemia or other cardiometabolic conditions may still be too high in fat for a true FCS diet, in which limiting fat intake to <20 g/day is recommended. … Specialized dietary programs that are personalized for the patient and developed in collaboration with a registered dietician can help develop sustainable eating habits. … Many diabetes diets have unsuitably high fat content for patients with FCS.
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Australian primary-care advice for severe hypertriglyceridaemia:** a low-fat diet with few added sugars, a very-low-fat diet once triglycerides exceed 10 mmol/L, dietitian referral, and no alcohol at all.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Standard triglyceride-lowering drugs (statins, fibrates, omega-3 fatty acids) are unlikely to help in FCS.** Avoid medicines that raise triglycerides, and treat hypothyroidism and uncontrolled diabetes.
claims.source_text: Common TG-lowering medications (eg, statins, fibrates, and omega-3 fatty acids) are unlikely to help patients with FCS … Medications that may increase TG levels (listed comprehensively in the NAFCS scoring system []) should be avoided. Comorbidities that raise TG levels, such as hypothyroidism and uncontrolled diabetes, should be investigated and treated
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **In severe hypertriglyceridaemia generally, Australian advice recommends fibrates** to lower triglycerides and pancreatitis risk; prescription omega-3 products may be considered. With a statin, fenofibrate is preferred to gemfibrozil.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Olezarsen, an APOC3 antisense drug, is approved as an add-on to diet in adults with FCS** (US FDA 2024; European Medicines Agency 2025, for genetically confirmed FCS). In the phase 3 Balance trial (66 patients) olezarsen 80 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks lowered triglycerides at 6 months.
claims.source_text: Subsequent research enabled the development of olezarsen, a hepatocyte-targeted triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated ASO approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2024 as an adjunct to diet to reduce TG levels in adult patients with FCS [,] and by the European Medicines Agency in 2025 as an adjunct to diet in adult patients for the treatment of genetically confirmed FCS … The phase 3 Balance trial assessed the efficacy and safety of olezarsen administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 53 weeks in 66 patients with genetically identified FCS (Table 1) []. The trial met the primary endpoint of reduction from baseline in TG levels following olezarsen 80 mg vs placebo after 6 months
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Olezarsen adverse effects in Balance:** injection-site reactions (19% vs 9% on placebo), lower platelet count (12% vs 4%) and joint pain (9% vs 0%). Hypersensitivity reactions were the commonest reason for stopping, per the US prescribing information.
claims.source_text: which included injection-site reactions (19% vs 9%), decreased platelet count (12% vs 4%), and arthralgia (9% vs 0%) … Per the prescribing information, the most common reason for treatment discontinuation was hypersensitivity reactions
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Olezarsen is not approved in pregnancy and children were excluded from its trial** and are ineligible. Triglycerides rise in the third trimester, raising pancreatitis risk in FCS.
claims.source_text: Pregnancy is relevant because rising TG levels during the third trimester may be severely elevated in FCS and increase the risk for acute pancreatitis []. Olezarsen is not approved for use in pregnancy, and there are currently no data on olezarsen in pregnant women or its presence in the breast milk of lactating women, its effects on the breastfed infant, or its impact on milk production … Pediatric patients were excluded from Balance and are ineligible for olezarsen
claims.locator: Bajaj A, Oral EA, Brown A, Gaudet D, Alexander VJ, Karwatowska-Prokopczuk E, Baum SJ, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (doi 10.1016/j.ajpc.2025.101352), 'Clinical considerations for the treatment of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome using a hepatic-targeted APOC3 antisense oligonucleotide', published 16 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686656/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **The Australian review describes APOC3- and ANGPTL3-targeted RNA therapies as still in advanced clinical development;** they lower triglycerides substantially and can reduce acute pancreatitis, including in chylomicronaemia syndrome.
claims.locator: Lan NSR, Nelson AJ, Brett T, Hespe CM, Watts GF, Nicholls SJ, Australian Journal of General Practice 54(11):800-804 (doi 10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535), 'Hypertriglyceridaemia: A practical approach for primary care', November 2025, https://doi.org/10.31128/AJGP-01-25-7535, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute pancreatitis in FCS:** admit for IV fluids, bowel rest, pain control and watching for organ failure. Nothing by mouth for at least 48 hours, then clear fluids for another 48 hours, then food as tolerated with fat under 20 g/day. Enteral tube feeding is not advised in FCS.
claims.source_text: An episode of acute pancreatitis necessitates hospitalization with aggressive intravenous hydration, initial bowel rest, pain control, and careful monitoring for organ failure [,]. Patients should receive intravenous fluids while refraining from oral intake for ≥48 h, with gradual attempts to introduce clear liquids orally; after clear liquids for an additional 48 h, patients can gradually advance to soft and whole foods as tolerated while maintaining a total fat intake of <20 g/day. Although clinical guidelines recommend enteral tube feeding within 24 h over parenteral nutrition in patients experiencing acute pancreatitis [,], this may be more appropriate for non-HTG-induced pancreatitis and is not advised for patients with FCS.

claims.claim: **IV insulin and plasmapheresis are not generally recommended for hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis;** insulin does not work when LPL is completely absent and can cause hypoglycaemia.
claims.source_text: Insulin infusions may stimulate LPL activity and lower TG levels in patients with insulin-deficient diabetes presenting with HTG due to insulin deficiency but are ineffective in those with complete LPL deficiency and can cause hypoglycemia … Both intravenous insulin and plasmapheresis are not generally recommended for HTG-induced acute pancreatitis

claims.claim: ⚠️ **FCS pancreatitis can be misread as alcohol-related, or pain as drug-seeking.** Contact the patient's FCS specialist at presentation.
claims.source_text: Patients with FCS presenting with acute pancreatitis may sometimes be misdiagnosed as HTG due to alcohol abuse or as drug-seeking behavior for reported chronic abdominal pain. Consultation with the patient's FCS specialist at the time of presentation may be helpful for making the correct diagnosis.

claims.claim: **Check triglycerides at least 4 times a year after pancreatitis or when levels are unstable, and at least twice a year when stable** (European FCS Expert Panel, as cited in S3). If triglycerides do not fall on treatment, review the diet and cut fat further.
claims.source_text: The European FCS Expert Panel recommends TG testing at least 4 times/year following pancreatitis in patients with unstable TG levels and at least twice a year in those with stable TG levels and no history of HTG-induced pancreatitis. Clinicians may consider monitoring TG levels and lipids more frequently during olezarsen treatment. If TG levels remain unchanged or increase, the patient's diet should be investigated, and the fat content further reduced if warranted.
